hints: Start at the white air space (the lumen) and work outwards. Notice the order of the layers and how each one looks under the microscope.

Remember the bronchus wall from inside to outside: ciliated epithelium with goblet cells, then a thin band of smooth muscle, then glands and plates of cartilage. Look for the long, wavy, pink-staining fibre layer.
walkthrough:
**Orientate yourself in the micrograph**

Think like you are inside the airway looking out. The large white area at the top left is the lumen where air flows.

The first dark lining touching the air is the epithelium, then you move deeper into the wall.

**Recall the bronchus wall structure**

A bronchus is supported and controlled by several tissues in order. From lumen outwards you expect: ciliated pseudostratified epithelium with goblet cells, smooth muscle to constrict the airway, submucosal glands, then cartilage for support.

**Match each label to its tissue**

Label D is the inner lining with cilia and goblet cells, so that is epithelium. Label C is the continuous, wavy band of densely packed spindle-shaped fibres just beneath it, which is classic smooth muscle. Label A is clusters of dark round secretory cells (glands) and label B is the pale tissue with cells in spaces, which is cartilage. So C is smooth muscle.

options.A: This is a cluster of submucosal secretory glands, with many round dark nuclei, that produce mucus, not contracting muscle fibres.
options.B: This is hyaline cartilage, recognised by the pale matrix with chondrocytes sitting in lacunae, which supports the bronchus.
options.C: This is smooth muscle, seen as a continuous wavy band of elongated spindle fibres just outside the epithelium that can constrict the airway.
options.D: This is the ciliated pseudostratified epithelium with goblet cells lining the lumen, not muscle.
